lead: PRAM (Parallel Random Access Machine) is an ideal shared-memory computer: P processors, one shared memory, lockstep steps, and unit-cost reads and writes. It exists so parallel algorithms can be compared without real network delay, caches or contention. EREW, CREW and CRCW are its variants. Only a few universities teach it in detail; it remains the standard analysis model for shared-memory algorithms.
prereq: You need: shared-memory architectures for one address space and Flynn's MIMD model for many processors.

blocks.text: PRAM has P processors, numbered 0 to P−1, and M shared cells. In one step each processor may read one cell, compute, and write one cell. All processors step together: the model is synchronous. Every read and write costs 1 time unit, whatever the address. The model has no interconnection network, so no message delay and no contention cost. PRAM is ideal, not hardware. Parallel time T(P) is the number of steps. Cost C(P) = T(P) × P processor-time units; cost is also called work. Real caches and barriers add time, so PRAM time is a best case.

blocks.where: T(P) is parallel time in steps; P is the number of processors; C is cost in processor-time units.

blocks.text: EREW (Exclusive Read, Exclusive Write): at most one processor reads a cell and at most one writes it per step. CREW (Concurrent Read, Exclusive Write): many may read one cell, but only one may write it. CRCW (Concurrent Read, Concurrent Write): many may read and many may write one cell. A CRCW write conflict needs a rule. Common: all writers must write the same value, else the result is undefined. Arbitrary: one writer wins, but the model does not say which. Priority: the highest-numbered processor wins.

A CRCW machine simulates EREW directly, because CRCW permits every EREW step. EREW must serialise a CRCW write conflict. For common, arbitrary and priority rules, a binary tree combine resolves P writes in ⌈log₂ P⌉ rounds. Concurrent reads use one read plus a broadcast tree, also ⌈log₂ P⌉ rounds. The variants differ by at most a logarithmic time factor here. State algorithms on the weakest variant that works.

blocks.where: P is the number of contending processors; ⌈⌉ rounds up to a whole number.

figure.caption: Eight processors P0–P7 all write to cell A. On EREW a tree combine halves the writers each round, 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, so 3 rounds and cost 3 × 8 = 24 processor-time units; priority CRCW settles the same write in 1 round, cost 8.

spec.aria: A binary tree whose eight leaves are processors P0 to P7 all writing cell A; each level of the tree is one combine round, halving the writers 8 to 4 to 2 to 1, giving 3 rounds on EREW against 1 round on priority CRCW.

examples.question: P = 8 processors all write to cell A in one step. (a) Under EREW with a binary-tree combine, how many rounds and what is the cost? (b) Under priority CRCW, how many rounds and what is the cost? One round = 1 time unit.
steps: 1. Tree combine halves the active values: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. Rounds = log₂ 8 = 3.
2. EREW time = 3 rounds × 1 time unit = 3 time units.
4. Priority CRCW resolves the write in 1 round; time = 1 time unit.
examples.answer: EREW: 3 rounds, cost 24 processor-time units. Priority CRCW: 1 round, cost 8 processor-time units.
examples.check:
import math
p = 8
rounds = int(math.log2(p))
erew_time = rounds
erew_cost = rounds * p
crcw_time = 1
crcw_cost = crcw_time * p
print(rounds)
print(erew_cost)
print(crcw_cost)

traps: PRAM is not hardware. A PRAM speedup is not a real speedup; it ignores network delay and memory contention.
CREW allows concurrent reads only. Many writers to one cell in one step is CRCW.
Time is steps; cost is steps × processors. If the question asks for cost, giving only time loses marks.
In a write conflict, common, arbitrary and priority are different rules. Do not answer one when another is asked.

quiz.q: Define PRAM and name its three main variants.
quiz.a: Ideal shared-memory model: P processors in lockstep, unit-cost reads and writes to one memory. Variants: EREW, CREW, CRCW.

quiz.q: Why is CREW less restrictive than EREW?
quiz.a: CREW allows many processors to read one cell in a step; EREW allows only one reader. CREW still allows only one writer.

quiz.q: P = 16 processors write to one cell. EREW combines them by a binary tree. How many rounds, and what is the cost at 1 time unit per round?
quiz.a: Rounds = log₂ 16 = 4. Time = 4 units. Cost = 4 × 16 = 64 processor-time units.

quiz.q: A PRAM algorithm has T = 10 steps on P = 100 processors, so cost = 1000 processor-time units. Why can a student not claim a real 100× speedup?
quiz.a: PRAM ignores network delay, memory contention and synchronisation, and real processors may sit idle. Cost 1000 also means the parallel work equals 1000 sequential steps in the model, which bounds useful speedup.

quiz.q: List the three common CRCW write-conflict rules.
Why does a CRCW machine simulate EREW with no extra time, while EREW simulation costs O(log P)?
quiz.a: CRCW permits every EREW step. EREW must serialise a write conflict, for example by a tree combine with log₂ P levels.

beyond: Not for the exam. PRAM leads to the bulk-synchronous parallel (BSP) model, which charges for communication rounds, and to work-depth analysis used for GPU algorithms. Search 'PRAM simulation', 'BSP model' and 'work-depth model'.
